source.title: Synthetic Eggs in Many Baskets: The Impact of Synthetic Data Diversity on LLM Fine-Tuning

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether supervised fine-tuning changes harmful-response behavior using different data and measures from the original studies: Dolly-derived human and synthetic datasets, RefusalBench prompts, and an LLM harmfulness judge. It also tests adversarial jailbreak prompts, but does not measure token-position KL or safety localization.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior findings about safety degradation and refusal mechanisms, but those cited results are not this study's results. It tests benign-data fine-tuning and adversarial prompting; it does not test harmful-example fine-tuning, per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefilling, decoding changes, parameter localization, or safety deepening.
record.test_reason: LoRA fine-tuning of Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct on benign Dolly data (human or synthetic responses) raises judged harmfulness on RefusalBench. This is close to the original benign-fine-tuning setup (Qi et al. also used Dolly and a 1–5 harmfulness judge), but with a different benchmark and judge (Llama-3.1-70B), so T2. The jailbreak prompts are persona-style prompt templates, not compliant-prefix prefills, suffixes or decoding changes, so V4 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that human-data fine-tuning strongly breaks safety guardrails but lowers output quality. Synthetic fine-tuning also removes guardrails (mainly visible under jailbreak prompts, weakly on plain RB) while preserving quality. Single-source small-model data and multi-source large-model data are especially problematic.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LoRA supervised fine-tuning on human Dolly data or synthetic responses generated from Dolly prompts, then evaluates harmfulness on RefusalBench and jailbreak-paired prompts. It does not use the original studies' targeted harmful-example fine-tuning setup or measure refusal as the primary metric.
record.method_sensitivity: Target model size, fine-tuning data source and source diversity, source-model size, and prompt condition (RB versus RB+J) change the reported safety outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla Llama-3.1 models are more often critically harmful when harmful queries are wrapped in persona jailbreak templates: 8B 1.25%→38.03%, 70B 5.45%→14.06%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generic prompt-template jailbreaks raise harmful compliance in safety-tuned models without fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic-data fine-tuning keeps output quality high while harmfulness rises, filling a high-quality/high-harm 'danger zone'. Human-data fine-tuning raises harm but lowers quality.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign-fine-tuning safety loss varies in actionability of harmful outputs depending on data source.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2026)
record.problems: Safety outcomes rely on an LLM judge, and the authors note that judge reliability varies and that a human-validation slice would strengthen confidence. Safety results are reported without uncertainty estimates in the cited comparisons. Target models are from one model family, and the study evaluates single-turn English prompts and LoRA-based SFT only.
record.rows_left_out: No additional version-relevant safety outcomes were omitted. The danger-zone measure combines harmfulness and response quality and was not entered as a direct harmful-compliance result.

untested.parts: No sweep over the amount of fine-tuning data or epochs, and no carefully selected benign subsets. Only LoRA SFT on one model family.
No prefill, adversarial-suffix or decoding attacks; only persona jailbreak templates.
Catastrophic forgetting of surface-layer safety is only speculated.

missing.what: Per-condition average harmfulness scores (single vs multi source, source size, human, vanilla) for both targets on RB and RB+J
Per-condition critically-harmful (score ≥4) rates for fine-tuned models, e.g. 8B single/multi RB+J 66.28%/59.44% vs vanilla 38.03%; 8B human RB 47.22%; 70B human RB 23.70%
missing.locator: Table D.2 and Appendix D.2 text

missing.what: Four of ten RB fine-tunes (all 70B) did not increase harmfulness; 70B multi-source-small decreased significantly
Five of six human- or small-single-source fine-tuned models gave critically harmful responses over 50% of the time

record.verdict_notes: The study's main focus is synthetic-data diversity; safety is a downstream case study. The judge is Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, which is also a target model, and no uncertainty is given on safety numbers. Table D.1/D.2 layout is garbled in the text extraction, so the column assignment of some 70B values is uncertain. The 8B and human values cited above match the authors' prose. The record's V4 links were removed because the jailbreak templates are not the bypass operations V4 names.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on harmful examples or measure whether a few to a few hundred such examples remove refusal.
Tests Dolly-derived human and synthetic instruction-response data, not a sweep over data counts or carefully selected benign subsets.
Tests jailbreak prompts combined with harmful queries, not compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes as a distinct intervention, or decoding changes.
LoRA is used for fine-tuning, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Offers a possible explanation involving distribution shifts and brittle surface-layer safety tuning, but does not experimentally test why safety would be shallow.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to spread safety beyond initial response tokens.
